idiom_name: Sequelize {lock: true, skipLocked} inside a transaction, or Knex .forUpdate()/.noWait()
implementation_notes: Sequelize turns lock: true on a query inside a managed transaction into FOR UPDATE and skipLocked: true into SKIP LOCKED, and Knex exposes forUpdate()/forShare()/noWait()/skipLocked() for PostgreSQL and MySQL; both release the row lock when the transaction commits. The offline lease is therefore a lock record claimed inside one short transaction - JavaScript supplies the primitive and the event loop, but a Node process cannot hold a database transaction across user think time without holding a pool connection for everybody. The classic lock-manager structure stays because the claim must survive between requests, not just between awaits.
pitfalls: Lock options only apply to queries executed with the transaction: forgetting { transaction: t } (or CLS) runs the query outside the lock and returns unprotected rows.
SQLite does not support more than one transaction at a time, so these code paths cannot be exercised against a SQLite test database.
Awaiting a row lock holds a pooled connection for the duration of the transaction, and the pool (not the lock) becomes the first thing to fail under contention.
